title: Fundamentals — Optimization (Junior)

tasks.title: The Withholding Select

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is building the daily Silver pipeline that reads Bronze meter readings, joins to the substations reference table, and writes a slim per-substation summary to Gold. The engineer's first cut works correctly and finishes in about 4 minutes on a 16-core cluster. A teammate notes the pipeline reads 8GB of Parquet for an output that needs only meter_id, substation_id, and daily_kw, and asks the engineer to look at the explain() output before merging.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is building the daily Silver pipeline that reads Bronze meter readings, joins to the substations reference table, and writes a slim per-substation summary to Gold. The engineer's first cut works correctly and finishes in about 4 minutes on a 16-core cluster. A teammate notes the pipeline reads 8GB of Parquet for an output that needs only meter_id, substation_id, and daily_kw, and asks the engineer to look at the explain() output before merging.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver-to-Gold step has a 5-minute SLA on the production cluster. The pipeline currently meets the SLA but reads more data than its output requires, leaving no margin when the meter count grows.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (20 rows, 6 columns), substations.csv (6 rows, 4 columns)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

meters = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
subs = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/substations/')

# load everything, then narrow at the end
df = meters.join(subs, 'substation_id', 'left')
df = df.filter(F.col('region') == 'NORTH')
df = df.select('meter_id', 'substation_id', 'daily_kw')
df.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/gold/north_summary/')

evidence.title: Expected Behavior
evidence.content: Read only the three columns needed (meter_id, substation_id, daily_kw) plus the partition column (region) for the filter. Total scan target: ~1.5GB of the 8GB Bronze table.

evidence.title: Observed Behavior
evidence.content: Spark UI shows the FileScan reads 8GB and the ReadSchema lists all 11 columns of the meters table. The filter pushes down (PartitionFilters: [region=NORTH]) but column pruning does not narrow the read.

fields.label: Why does the FileScan read all 11 columns instead of only the three the output uses?
options: The filter on region runs before the select, so Spark must read every column to evaluate the filter expression on the meters DataFrame in the join.
Parquet stores columns together in row groups, so any read of a row group materialises every column the row group contains as part of the scan.
The join is performed on the wide meters DataFrame before the select narrows it, so the read needs every column the join's downstream operators might still reference.
Catalyst inferred the schema from the Parquet footer at planning time and the inferred schema includes all 11 columns regardless of which select calls follow it.
fields.correctAnswer: The join is performed on the wide meters DataFrame before the select narrows it, so the read needs every column the join's downstream operators might still reference.
fields.rationale:
Operator order in the chain matters. Until the terminal select runs, the chain still has a wide DataFrame on the join's left side, and the projection-pushdown rule needs to see the narrow column set above the FileScan to push it through. The filter pushes down independently, Parquet's row-group layout does not block per-column skipping, and schema inference establishes what is available, not what is read.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer had written the select on the meters DataFrame BEFORE the join, option C's diagnosis would not apply because the chain would already carry the narrow set. The exercise's framing (terminal select after the join) is what makes the operator order the cause.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Conflates filter pushdown with projection pushdown; the filter pushes down independently of how many columns the read returns.

Option B: Mistakes Parquet's physical layout for the limit on Spark's column skipping; the reader skips columns within a row group.

Option D: Confuses schema inference (what columns exist) with read planning (which columns are read).

fields.label: Which single-line edit gives Catalyst the information it needs to prune to three columns at the file scan?
options: Insert a select for the three needed columns plus region on the meters DataFrame BEFORE the join, so the join's input already carries only the columns the output requires.
Move the existing terminal select up so it runs immediately after the filter and before the write, narrowing the projection one stage earlier in the chain.
Add a cache call on the meters DataFrame after the read so Catalyst sees the materialisation point and prunes the columns the cache holds in memory.
Pass a columns list to the spark.read.parquet call so the reader receives the projection at construction and avoids planning the scan over unused columns.
fields.correctAnswer: Insert a select for the three needed columns plus region on the meters DataFrame BEFORE the join, so the join's input already carries only the columns the output requires.
fields.rationale:
Putting the projection on meters before the join lets Catalyst see the three-column shape on the left side, and that shape propagates down to the FileScan. Region is included so the partition filter still evaluates. Moving the existing select up (option B) does not help because the join is what locks in the column set. Cache adds memory cost without enabling pruning, and spark.read.parquet does not accept a columns argument.

When this answer is wrong: If the join were a broadcast of subs onto meters and the engineer wanted to keep all meter columns available downstream, option B's narrower change would be correct because the wide left side is the desired carrier. The exercise's framing (output needs only three columns) makes the early select the right edit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats the select's position relative to the filter as the issue; the join is what locks in the column set.

Option C: Reaches for cache as a tuning lever; cache adds memory cost and does not enable pruning.

Option D: Invents a parameter the reader API does not accept; projection comes from select, not the read call.

fields.label: The teammate suggests replacing 'meters.join(subs, ...)' with 'meters.select(...).join(subs, ...)'. Which best explains why this change works for column pruning?
options: The select inserted before the join shrinks the join's left-side input row width, which lets the join operator process more rows per executor task without spilling.
The select forces Spark to materialise an intermediate table that the join reads from, breaking the lazy chain and making the pruned columns visible to the planner.
The select adds a Project node after the FileScan and Catalyst pushes the Project down through the FileScan, which lets the reader skip column groups not in the projection.
Catalyst's projection-pushdown rule sees the narrow column set required above the FileScan and configures the Parquet reader to read only those columns from disk.
fields.correctAnswer: Catalyst's projection-pushdown rule sees the narrow column set required above the FileScan and configures the Parquet reader to read only those columns from disk.
fields.rationale:
Pruning happens because Catalyst propagates the column requirement down to the data source; the rule examines what is referenced above the scan, intersects it with what the source can supply, and tells the file reader which fields to materialise. The narrower row width is a true side effect but not the cause. Select is lazy and does not materialise. The Project node itself is not pushed through the FileScan; only the column requirement is.

When this answer is wrong: If the data source were a CSV file (which has no per-column read), the rule would still propagate the column requirement but the reader could not skip columns at the I/O layer. The exercise's framing (Parquet) is what makes the at-the-reader pruning the relevant mechanism.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names a downstream effect (narrower rows) and treats it as the cause of the upstream change (column pruning).

Option B: Assumes select is eager when it is lazy; no materialisation happens.

Option C: Inverts the mechanism: the Project itself is not pushed down, the column requirement is propagated to the scan.

fields.label: After the fix, the engineer reruns and the Spark UI shows ReadSchema: [meter_id, substation_id, daily_kw, region]. Why does region appear even though the output does not use it?
options: Region is the table's partition column and Parquet stores the partition value in the file path; the reader includes it free without reading any column data from the files.
Region is needed at planning time to evaluate the filter expression, so Catalyst keeps it in the read schema even after the select that excludes it from the join's output.
Region was selected indirectly because the substations DataFrame contains a region column with the same name and the join key resolution pulled it into the meters scan.
Region is included in the read schema as a side effect of partition discovery; Spark added it to the schema during the directory listing that precedes the file scan.
fields.correctAnswer: Region is the table's partition column and Parquet stores the partition value in the file path; the reader includes it free without reading any column data from the files.
fields.rationale:
Partition columns are encoded in the directory path (e.g., region=NORTH) and the reader gets them by parsing the path, not by reading file content. Spark lists region in the read schema for plan readability, but no extra column I/O happens for it. The filter has already been resolved at directory level, the snippet has no name collision with substations, and partition discovery is a planning step, not a per-file read.

When this answer is wrong: If region were a regular column (not a partition column), option B's diagnosis would describe a real cost: the reader would have to materialise region to evaluate the filter. The exercise's framing (region is the partition column) makes the cost free.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats the filter as if it ran at the scan; partition filters resolve before any file is opened.

Option C: Invents a same-name collision in the substations join that the snippet does not have.

Option D: Conflates partition discovery (a planning step) with the scan's per-file column read.

fields.label: Suppose the engineer adds a withColumn that derives reading_grade from daily_kw before the terminal select. What happens to the read schema?
options: The withColumn introduces a Project node that Catalyst does not push past the FileScan, so the read schema falls back to all 11 columns of the meters Parquet table.
The withColumn shifts the scan to read all columns referenced anywhere in the chain, which adds reading_grade as a virtual column and triggers a full scan in the process.
The read schema is unchanged because reading_grade depends only on daily_kw, which is already in the projection, and Catalyst's pruning sees the same minimal column set.
The read schema gains reading_grade because Catalyst includes derived columns in the FileScan's projection so the executor can compute them as part of the read step.
fields.correctAnswer: The read schema is unchanged because reading_grade depends only on daily_kw, which is already in the projection, and Catalyst's pruning sees the same minimal column set.
fields.rationale:
Pruning tracks the columns the chain actually reads, not the columns it derives. reading_grade is computed from daily_kw, and daily_kw is already in the projection from the terminal select; no new column has to come out of the file. Catalyst still pushes Project nodes through FileScans even when derived values are introduced, and derivations happen in the executor after the read.

When this answer is wrong: If the withColumn referenced a column not in the existing projection (e.g., a derivation from temperature_c), the read schema would gain that column to supply the input. The exercise's framing (derivation from daily_kw) keeps the projection minimal.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Asserts that withColumn breaks projection pushdown when it does not; the rule still fires.

Option B: Inverts the relationship: derived columns do not widen the read; they consume already-projected ones.

Option D: Places the derivation at the read step; derivations happen at the executor after columns are read.

tasks.pssReference: Junior PS3 (DataFrames and lazy evaluation), Junior PS4 (Selecting), Junior PS8 (Reading and Writing); Optimization Cross-Track OPT-J1 lesson 3, OPT-J2 lesson 1.

tasks.title: The Filter That Stayed Put

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is debugging a Bronze-to-Silver pipeline that scans 12GB instead of the 800MB the team expects. The Bronze table is partitioned by date, and the engineer's query is supposed to read only one date. The pipeline produces correct output but reads sixteen times more data than needed. A quick look at the explain() shows the date predicate appears in the Filter node above the FileScan but does not appear in PartitionFilters at the scan itself.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is debugging a Bronze-to-Silver pipeline that scans 12GB instead of the 800MB the team expects. The Bronze table is partitioned by date, and the engineer's query is supposed to read only one date. The pipeline produces correct output but reads sixteen times more data than needed. A quick look at the explain() shows the date predicate appears in the Filter node above the FileScan but does not appear in PartitionFilters at the scan itself.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Bronze layer is read by twelve downstream pipelines daily. Read amplification on this pipeline costs cluster minutes that show up on the team's monthly bill, and the missing partition pruning is the difference between a 25-second scan and a 6-minute scan.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Bronze layer is partitioned by date)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

target_date = '2026-03-15'

bronze = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
bronze = bronze.withColumn(
    'is_target',
    F.when(F.col('date') == target_date, F.lit(True)).otherwise(F.lit(False))
)
silver = bronze.filter(F.col('is_target')).select('meter_id', 'date', 'daily_kw')
silver.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/silver/meters/2026-03-15/')

evidence.title: Expected Behavior
evidence.content: Catalyst pushes the date predicate down to the FileScan as a PartitionFilter so only the date=2026-03-15 directory is read (~800MB).

evidence.title: Observed Behavior
evidence.content: PartitionFilters is empty in the plan. ReadSchema includes is_target. The scan reads all 30 daily directories (~12GB) and the filter applies after the read.

fields.label: Why does Catalyst fail to push the date predicate down to PartitionFilters?
options: The filter checks is_target rather than date, and is_target is a derived column that does not exist on the Parquet file system, so Catalyst has no partition path to match the predicate against during planning.

The filter operator runs after the withColumn step, and Catalyst applies pushdown rules in the order the chain declares them rather than reordering filters past intermediate withColumn steps that hold on to the predicate.

The when expression that defines is_target wraps the date comparison inside a conditional, and Catalyst does not unwrap conditional expressions to extract pushable predicates from inside the branch arms during planning.

The filter compares against a Python variable target_date that the planner sees as a runtime value, and pushdown to PartitionFilters works only on literal expressions known at compile time inside the filter call itself.
fields.correctAnswer: The filter operator runs after the withColumn step, and Catalyst applies pushdown rules in the order the chain declares them rather than reordering filters past intermediate withColumn steps that hold on to the predicate.
fields.rationale:
When Catalyst processes the chain, it tries to push pushable predicates down through projections. Here the predicate sits on is_target, a column produced by withColumn, so what reaches the FileScan is a filter on a derived column the file system has no notion of. The conditional unwrapping mentioned in option C is something some optimisers do but is not the proximate cause; the Python variable in option D is folded to a literal at planning; option A states a true fact (is_target does not exist on disk) but pins the failure on the wrong link in the chain.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer had written a direct filter on date alongside the withColumn (rather than relying on is_target), the predicate would push down even with the derived column present. The exercise's framing (filter on is_target only) is what blocks the pushdown.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names a true fact about is_target but blames the file system rather than the chain order that hides the underlying date predicate.

Option C: Asserts a generic limitation on conditional unwrapping; Catalyst does extract simple equality from when in some versions, and this is not the documented blocker here.

Option D: Assumes Python variables block pushdown; they are folded to literals at plan time and do not interfere.

fields.label: Which single edit restores partition pruning without changing the output of the pipeline?
options: Replace the when expression with a coalesce of date and a literal, then use the result column as the filter predicate so Catalyst sees a stable column reference at the filter step.
Move the withColumn step to run after the select so Catalyst's pushdown rule applies to a chain in which the filter sits directly above the FileScan with no intermediate projection.
Replace the existing filter with a direct predicate on date, dropping the is_target derivation entirely; the comparison against the partition column is what enables pushdown to PartitionFilters.
Add a hint that requests partition pruning on the date column before the withColumn runs, which gives Catalyst an explicit instruction to extract the predicate from the conditional.
fields.correctAnswer: Replace the existing filter with a direct predicate on date, dropping the is_target derivation entirely; the comparison against the partition column is what enables pushdown to PartitionFilters.
fields.rationale:
The cleanest fix is to filter directly on date because that is the partition column. The is_target column was an indirection that hid a perfectly pushable predicate. Coalescing with a literal does not produce a pushable form. Reordering withColumn after select does not help because withColumn referencing date would still leave is_target as the filter target. There is no hint that asks Catalyst to extract a predicate from a conditional.

When this answer is wrong: If is_target were used by other operators downstream (e.g., a join condition), removing it entirely would break those operators and the engineer would need to keep both the derivation and a separate direct date filter. The exercise's framing (is_target used only for the filter) makes the direct fix the right one.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats coalesce as a way to expose a predicate; it produces a different expression that is also not pushable.

Option B: Reorders steps in a way that does not address the indirection through is_target.

Option D: Invents a hint API that does not exist; pushdown is rule-driven, not hint-driven.

fields.label: After the fix, the engineer wants to keep an is_target boolean for an audit log that the team writes alongside the silver output. Which placement preserves partition pruning?
options: Add the withColumn after the partition filter on date so the derivation runs only on the rows that survive the pruned scan and the filter still pushes down at the FileScan.
Add the withColumn before the filter and add a second filter on date in addition to the is_target filter so Catalyst sees the pushable predicate at the filter step alongside the derived one.
Add the withColumn after the filter on is_target so the derivation is computed only after pruning has happened, matching the chain order Catalyst inspects when applying its rule.
Add the withColumn before the read by passing it as a transform option to spark.read.parquet so the derivation happens inside the reader and never participates in the filter chain at all.
fields.correctAnswer: Add the withColumn after the partition filter on date so the derivation runs only on the rows that survive the pruned scan and the filter still pushes down at the FileScan.
fields.rationale:
Putting the derivation after the filter means the partition pruning happens first and only the surviving rows feed the withColumn. The filter remains a direct predicate on the partition column, which is what the rule needs. Option B works mechanically but adds a redundant operator; option C contradicts the previous question because it brings is_target back as the filter target; option D invents a transform option the reader API does not expose.

When this answer is wrong: If the audit log requires is_target for both the kept rows and the discarded ones (i.e., it logs which rows did NOT match), the derivation must run before the filter, and the engineer would need a separate direct date filter to preserve pushdown. The exercise's framing (audit log alongside silver output) keeps is_target only on the kept rows.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Reaches for two filters when one (after the derivation) is the same fix proposed for the previous question.

Option C: Reintroduces the indirection through is_target that was the original problem.

Option D: Invents a reader-level transform option that is not part of the Parquet source API.

fields.label: The fix is shipped. PartitionFilters now shows [date=2026-03-15] and the scan reads ~800MB. Which other plan field most directly confirms the pruning worked at the directory level?
options: ReadSchema, which now lists only the columns the select projects, confirming Spark narrowed both the column projection and the partition reading at the scan operator level.
Number of partitions read, shown as the count of input directories the FileScan opened; one partition read confirms the planner skipped the other twenty-nine date directories on disk.
PushedFilters, which now lists the date equality predicate, confirming Spark sent the filter to the Parquet reader at the file level rather than only at the directory listing step.
Output rows estimate, shown as one-thirtieth of the original Bronze row count, confirming the cost-based optimiser reduced its row count estimate to match the pruned partition input.
fields.correctAnswer: Number of partitions read, shown as the count of input directories the FileScan opened; one partition read confirms the planner skipped the other twenty-nine date directories on disk.
fields.rationale:
The directory-skipping evidence sits in the per-scan input counter that the SQL DAG reports under the FileScan; one input directory means twenty-nine were skipped on disk. PushedFilters records predicates pushed to the file (row-group) level, which is a different mechanism from PartitionFilters. ReadSchema confirms column pruning, not partition pruning. The output-row estimate is a planner figure that does not by itself confirm the directories were skipped on disk.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer is verifying file-level row-group skipping (as opposed to directory-level partition skipping), PushedFilters is the relevant evidence because it shows what the Parquet reader applied. The exercise's framing (directory-level pruning by date) makes the partitions-read counter the direct confirmation.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Conflates column pruning evidence with partition pruning evidence; both are pruning but at different layers.

Option C: Treats PushedFilters as evidence of directory skipping; it documents file-level filter application.

Option D: Reads the optimiser's estimate as evidence of physical scan behaviour; the estimate is a planning figure.

tasks.title: Did the Pushdown Happen?

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is comparing two near-identical queries against the Bronze meters Parquet table. The two queries return the same rows but the runtimes differ by a factor of nine. The team's lead asks the engineer to read the explain() output for each and identify which one pushed the predicate down to the Parquet reader and which one did not. The Bronze table is partitioned by date and stored as plain Parquet (not Delta).
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is comparing two near-identical queries against the Bronze meters Parquet table. The two queries return the same rows but the runtimes differ by a factor of nine. The team's lead asks the engineer to read the explain() output for each and identify which one pushed the predicate down to the Parquet reader and which one did not. The Bronze table is partitioned by date and stored as plain Parquet (not Delta).

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The slow query is on a developer's hot-loop iteration path. Cutting it from 45 seconds to 5 seconds saves the developer enough time across a working day that the team treats it as a productivity-grade optimisation, not just a performance one.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Bronze partitioned by date)

evidence.label: Query A
evidence.content:
df = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
result = df.filter(df.date == '2026-03-15').filter(df.daily_kw > 1000).select('meter_id', 'daily_kw')

evidence.label: Query B
evidence.content:
df = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
df = df.withColumn('daily_kw_norm', df.daily_kw / 1000.0)
result = df.filter(df.date == '2026-03-15').filter(df.daily_kw_norm > 1.0).select('meter_id', 'daily_kw_norm')

evidence.label: Plan A
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [meter_id, daily_kw]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw) AND (daily_kw > 1000.0))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [meter_id, daily_kw, date]
         Batched: true, DataFilters: [isnotnull(daily_kw), (daily_kw > 1000.0)],
         Format: Parquet, PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(date), (date = 2026-03-15)],
         PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw, 1000.0)],
         ReadSchema: struct<meter_id:string, daily_kw:double>

evidence.label: Plan B
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [meter_id, (daily_kw / 1000.0) AS daily_kw_norm]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw) AND ((daily_kw / 1000.0) > 1.0))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [meter_id, daily_kw, date]
         Batched: true, DataFilters: [isnotnull(daily_kw)],
         Format: Parquet, PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(date), (date = 2026-03-15)],
         PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw)],
         ReadSchema: struct<meter_id:string, daily_kw:double>

fields.label: Which plan field tells you the daily_kw threshold predicate was sent into the Parquet reader for query A?
options: PushedFilters lists GreaterThan(daily_kw, 1000.0), which is the form the Parquet reader interprets to skip row groups whose statistics show no values can satisfy the predicate at file read time.
DataFilters lists the daily_kw threshold expression, which records that the Filter operator above the scan applies the predicate to each row Spark reads from the Parquet files.
PartitionFilters lists the predicate alongside the date predicate, which records that Spark uses both predicates together at the directory listing step before any file is opened.
The Project node references daily_kw, which records that Spark reads the column out of the Parquet files and applies the threshold during the columnar-to-row conversion at the scan boundary.
fields.correctAnswer: PushedFilters lists GreaterThan(daily_kw, 1000.0), which is the form the Parquet reader interprets to skip row groups whose statistics show no values can satisfy the predicate at file read time.
fields.rationale:
PushedFilters is the field that lists predicates sent into the data source, where the Parquet reader can use min/max statistics in the row-group metadata to skip whole row groups. DataFilters records what the Filter operator applies above the scan; the predicate appears there too in plan A, but that field documents row-by-row work, not row-group skipping. PartitionFilters tracks directory-level pruning, not file-level row-group pushdown. The Project node lists projection, not predicates.

When this answer is wrong: If the data source were a CSV (which has no per-row-group statistics), the same predicate would still appear in DataFilters and not in PushedFilters; the pushdown evidence would be absent because CSV cannot use it. The exercise's framing (Parquet) is what makes PushedFilters the relevant field.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Confuses the row-by-row filter the operator applies with the row-group skipping the reader applies; DataFilters documents the former.

Option C: Treats partition pruning and row-group pushdown as the same mechanism; they happen at different layers.

Option D: Reads the Project node as if it carried predicates; it documents which columns survive.

fields.label: Why does plan B not list a daily_kw_norm threshold in PushedFilters?
options: The Parquet reader rejects predicates with floating-point operands because comparison semantics differ between the file format and the JVM, so divisions like daily_kw_norm are evaluated only above the scan.
The Parquet reader accepts predicates only on columns that exist as fields in the file schema, and daily_kw_norm is a derived column that does not exist in the meters Parquet files at the read step.

Catalyst applies pushdown only to the first filter in the chain after the scan, and daily_kw_norm appears in the second filter, so the rule has already finished running by the time it reaches the second filter.

PushedFilters tracks predicates that survived the Catalyst rule that combines adjacent filters into one, and the daily_kw_norm filter merged into the date filter, removing it from the pushable predicate set.
fields.correctAnswer: Catalyst applies pushdown only to the first filter in the chain after the scan, and daily_kw_norm appears in the second filter, so the rule has already finished running by the time it reaches the second filter.
fields.rationale:
PushedFilters can only carry predicates that reference columns the data source actually has. daily_kw_norm is computed by withColumn at execution time and is not a field in the Parquet files. The reader has no value to compare against, so the predicate stays above the scan. The reader does accept floating-point predicates, the order-of-rule-application story does not match how Catalyst applies pushdown, and there is no Catalyst rule that drops predicates by merging filters.

When this answer is wrong: If daily_kw_norm were materialised as a real column in a separate Parquet table that the engineer then queried, the predicate would push down because the column would exist in the file schema. The exercise's framing (derived at execution time) is what blocks pushdown.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a floating-point semantics block; the reader handles double comparisons routinely.

Option B: States the right consequence (predicate stays above the scan) but pins it on rule order rather than on the column not existing.

Option D: Misreads the filter-combination rule; it merges filters into one predicate and does not drop predicates from the pushable set.

fields.label: Both plans show ReadSchema: struct<meter_id:string, daily_kw:double>. What does this confirm?
options: Both queries projected the date column out of the read because the partition filter consumed it during planning, leaving only the columns referenced by the surviving operators above the scan.
Both queries narrowed the Parquet column read to the two columns each one actually uses; column pruning works for both even though plan B has the additional derived column above the scan.
Both queries produced identical physical plans because Catalyst's rules normalise away the syntactic difference between filtering on daily_kw directly and filtering on daily_kw_norm in the chain.
Both queries forced the reader to load only daily_kw and meter_id, but the Parquet column index is consulted at read time using the values listed in PushedFilters before the load happens.
fields.correctAnswer: Both queries narrowed the Parquet column read to the two columns each one actually uses; column pruning works for both even though plan B has the additional derived column above the scan.
fields.rationale:
ReadSchema records the columns the reader materialises from the files. Both queries list meter_id and daily_kw, so column pruning fired in each case. Plan B's daily_kw_norm derivation is computed above the scan from the already-read daily_kw column. The two plans are not identical (PushedFilters differs), the date column appears as a partition column not via projection, and the Parquet column index is not consulted by ReadSchema.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer changed the projection in plan B to include daily_kw alongside daily_kw_norm, ReadSchema would not change because daily_kw is already read; the engineer might mistakenly conclude that pruning behaviour changed. The exercise's framing (both plans show the same ReadSchema) makes pruning the direct read.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reaches for partition projection logic when ReadSchema documents the file column read.

Option C: Asserts plan equivalence when PushedFilters clearly differs between the two plans.

Option D: Conflates ReadSchema (column read scope) with how Parquet uses statistics during file open.

fields.label: Which line in plan A confirms that only the 2026-03-15 directory was opened, regardless of how the file-level pushdown applied?
options: The DataFilters line, which carries the predicate alongside the row-group statistics that the FileScan operator uses to decide which directories to list during planning.
The PartitionFilters line, which records the predicates Spark evaluated against the partition values encoded in the directory paths before opening any files at all.
The ReadSchema line, which lists only the non-partition columns and confirms by omission that the date partition column was resolved at the directory listing step.
The PushedFilters line on the daily_kw predicate, which confirms by sequence that the date predicate was evaluated earlier and limited the listing to the 2026-03-15 directory.
fields.correctAnswer: The PartitionFilters line, which records the predicates Spark evaluated against the partition values encoded in the directory paths before opening any files at all.
fields.rationale:
Directory-level pruning is what PartitionFilters records. The line lists the date predicate and Spark uses it during partition discovery, before any file is opened. DataFilters documents row-by-row work after the scan. ReadSchema documents which columns are read; it does not by itself say which directories were opened. PushedFilters documents file-level row-group skipping for the daily_kw predicate, which is a different layer.

When this answer is wrong: If the table were not partitioned by date (a common case where the predicate column is just a regular column), PartitionFilters would be empty and the only directory-level evidence would come from a different mechanism, dynamic partition pruning. The exercise's framing (table partitioned by date) makes PartitionFilters the direct evidence.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Maps row-group statistics to directory listing; the two operate at different layers.

Option C: Treats omission from ReadSchema as confirmation of directory pruning; the omission documents the column projection, not the listing scope.

Option D: Reads PushedFilters as a sequencing record across predicates; it documents what each predicate did at the file level.

fields.label: Suppose the engineer rewrites query B to use 'daily_kw > 1000.0' instead of 'daily_kw_norm > 1.0' (keeping the withColumn that derives daily_kw_norm for the output). What changes in plan B?
options: PushedFilters loses the IsNotNull entry because the rewritten predicate no longer triggers the null check that the Parquet reader injects when comparing a derived column to a literal of a different precision.

The Project node above the Filter expands to include the derivation expression so the daily_kw_norm column is materialised after the threshold filter runs against the original daily_kw column at the scan.
ReadSchema stays the same because the read still needs daily_kw and meter_id and the change touches only the predicate the reader gets, not the columns it materialises during the scan.
PushedFilters gains a new entry for the daily_kw threshold matching the entry in plan A; the rewrite exposes the predicate on the actual file column instead of on the derived one.
fields.correctAnswer: PushedFilters gains a new entry for the daily_kw threshold matching the entry in plan A; the rewrite exposes the predicate on the actual file column instead of on the derived one.
fields.rationale:
The rewrite places the threshold on daily_kw, which the file schema does have, so PushedFilters now matches plan A. The withColumn for daily_kw_norm still runs but only as a projection above the filter, on the rows that survived the pushed predicate. PushedFilters does not lose its IsNotNull entry, the Project node does not gain the threshold filter, and ReadSchema stays the same because the same columns were already needed.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer kept the filter on daily_kw_norm but materialised daily_kw_norm as a real column in a precomputed Parquet table, PushedFilters would gain GreaterThan(daily_kw_norm, 1.0) instead. The exercise's framing (rewrite the predicate on the original column) makes the daily_kw entry the change.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a null-check behaviour tied to derived columns that the reader does not implement that way.

Option B: Moves the projection inside the filter step; Project remains above the filter and just keeps the derivation.

Option C: States a true fact about ReadSchema but as the answer to what changed; the question asks what changes, and PushedFilters is what does.

tasks.pssReference: Junior PS3 (lazy evaluation/explain), Junior PS4 (Filtering); Mid PSI1 lessons 4-5 (predicate pushdown, partition pruning); Optimization Cross-Track OPT-J1 lesson 7, OPT-J2 lesson 2.

tasks.title: Counting Shuffles in a Five-Step Plan

description.context: A NordGrid engineer wrote a 30-line Silver pipeline that reads meters, joins to substations, computes a per-region daily total, deduplicates against a quality lookup, and writes a Gold table. The pipeline finishes in 11 minutes. The engineer suspects one of the operations is causing a shuffle that is not strictly necessary. The lead asks the engineer to read the physical plan and count Exchange nodes, name what each one is for, and identify which one (if any) could be eliminated.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer wrote a 30-line Silver pipeline that reads meters, joins to substations, computes a per-region daily total, deduplicates against a quality lookup, and writes a Gold table. The pipeline finishes in 11 minutes. The engineer suspects one of the operations is causing a shuffle that is not strictly necessary. The lead asks the engineer to read the physical plan and count Exchange nodes, name what each one is for, and identify which one (if any) could be eliminated.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: Every shuffle in this pipeline writes between 600MB and 4GB of data through the network and back to disk on the cluster. Eliminating one unnecessary shuffle saves five to seven minutes of stage time and the corresponding executor memory pressure.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv, substations.csv (small reference table)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
meters = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/')
subs = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/substations/')
quality = spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/quality/')

joined = meters.join(subs, 'substation_id', 'left')
filtered = joined.filter(F.col('region') == 'NORTH')
agg = filtered.groupBy('region', 'date').agg(F.sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'))
deduped = agg.join(quality, ['region', 'date'], 'left').dropDuplicates(['region', 'date'])
deduped.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/gold/north_daily/')

evidence.label: Physical Plan
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(7) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)        [E3]
   +- *(6) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[partial_first])
      +- *(6) Project [region, date, total_kw, quality_flag]
         +- *(6) SortMergeJoin [region, date], [region, date], LeftOuter
            :- *(3) Sort [region, date]
            :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)        [E2]
            :     +- *(2) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
            :        +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)  [E1]
            :           +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[region, date], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw)])
            :              +- *(1) BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id], [substation_id], LeftOuter, BuildRight
            :                 :- *(1) Filter (region = NORTH)
            :                 :  +- FileScan parquet meters
            :                 +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode             [B1]
            :                    +- FileScan parquet subs
            +- *(5) Sort [region, date]
               +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, date, 200)        [E4]
                  +- FileScan parquet quality

fields.label: How many shuffle Exchange nodes (excluding the broadcast exchange) does the plan contain?
options: Three Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan, with one for each of the user-visible operations the chain expresses: the groupBy step, the join step, and the dropDuplicates step at the end.

Four Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan: the partial sum produces one, the join requires one on each side of the sort-merge step, and the dropDuplicates produces one before the final aggregate.
Two Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan, since Catalyst combined the groupBy and the dropDuplicates into a single shuffle stage and reused the post-aggregate distribution.
Five Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan, since each of the read steps and each of the join steps issues its own Exchange in the SortMergeJoin sequence above the partial aggregates.
fields.correctAnswer: Four Exchange nodes drive shuffles in this plan: the partial sum produces one, the join requires one on each side of the sort-merge step, and the dropDuplicates produces one before the final aggregate.
fields.rationale:
The plan shows four Exchange nodes labelled E1–E4. E1 sits above the partial aggregate of the groupBy. E2 redistributes the aggregate output for the join with quality. E3 is the post-join shuffle that feeds the final HashAggregate (the dropDuplicates). E4 redistributes quality on the same keys for the SortMergeJoin. The other options either undercount the join's two-sided shuffles, mistake combination for elimination, or overcount by including reads.

When this answer is wrong: If AQE were enabled and post-shuffle coalescing reduced E1 and E2 into a single combined Exchange, the count could effectively be three at runtime. The exercise's framing (static physical plan) keeps the count at four.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Counts at the source-code-operation level, not the plan-operator level; the join contributes two Exchanges, not one.

Option C: Asserts a Catalyst combination rule that does not apply here; the two HashAggregates remain separate operators.

Option D: Counts FileScan reads as shuffles; reads are not Exchanges.

fields.label: Which Exchange (E1, E2, E3, or E4) corresponds to the dropDuplicates step in the source code?
options: E2 corresponds to dropDuplicates because the chain emits the deduplication after the aggregate and the second Exchange in the plan tree appears immediately above the partial aggregate at that level of the chain.

E3 corresponds to dropDuplicates because Catalyst implements dropDuplicates as a HashAggregate with first-on-each-key semantics, and E3 sits below the outer HashAggregate that produces the final output.
E4 corresponds to dropDuplicates because it sits on the right side of the SortMergeJoin and the deduplication needs to align both sides on the deduplication key before the join produces output.
E1 corresponds to dropDuplicates because the partial aggregate at the lowest level of the plan represents the deduplication step that runs before any other shuffle in the pipeline executes.
fields.correctAnswer: E1 corresponds to dropDuplicates because the partial aggregate at the lowest level of the plan represents the deduplication step that runs before any other shuffle in the pipeline executes.
fields.rationale:
Reading the plan carefully, the outer HashAggregate at the top has functions=[] (no aggregation function), which is how Catalyst implements dropDuplicates. The Exchange directly below it is E3. The wrong options pick neighbouring exchanges by position in the chain rather than by what each Exchange feeds. E1 feeds the partial-sum aggregate (groupBy), E2 feeds the SortMergeJoin's left side, E4 feeds its right side, and E3 feeds the final empty-functions HashAggregate.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer used distinct() instead of dropDuplicates(), the plan would show the same operator structure (HashAggregate with empty functions) and the same answer would apply. The exercise's framing identifies E3 specifically by its position above the empty-functions aggregate.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks E2 because dropDuplicates is the second-to-last source operation, conflating source order with plan order.

Option B: Names the right E3 in the prompt but for the wrong reason — credits a sequencing logic instead of identifying the empty-functions HashAggregate signature.

Option C: Picks E4 because it appears late in the plan tree, missing that E4 belongs to the right side of the join, not to dropDuplicates.

fields.label: The engineer notices that the dropDuplicates step uses the same key as the groupBy step. Which observation about this redundancy is correct?
options: The aggregate already produces unique (region, date) pairs because groupBy is one-row-per-key, and dropDuplicates on those same keys is a no-op that the optimiser cannot recognise on its own across an intervening join.

The aggregate produces one row per pair only when the input partitioning matches the keys, so dropDuplicates is the safety net that handles cases where a downstream shuffle reorders the rows in a non-key-preserving way.

The aggregate produces unique pairs but the join with quality may introduce duplicates if the quality table has multiple rows per pair, which is what the dropDuplicates after the join is genuinely guarding against in this plan.

The aggregate produces unique pairs but the broadcast of subs may emit one row per substation per pair, which Catalyst counts as duplicates that dropDuplicates removes after the SortMergeJoin to quality has run.
fields.correctAnswer: The aggregate already produces unique (region, date) pairs because groupBy is one-row-per-key, and dropDuplicates on those same keys is a no-op that the optimiser cannot recognise on its own across an intervening join.
fields.rationale:
After the groupBy on (region, date), each pair appears exactly once. The join with quality cannot introduce duplicates if quality has at most one row per pair (this is the assumption the next question makes explicit). dropDuplicates on (region, date) at this point is a no-op, but Catalyst cannot prove it without a uniqueness contract on the join input. The other options invent guard conditions or downstream effects that the plan does not actually have.

When this answer is wrong: If quality had multiple rows per (region, date) pair (a many-rows-per-key reference), option C's diagnosis would correctly identify a real risk that dropDuplicates is guarding against. The exercise's framing (next question) makes the at-most-one-per-pair contract explicit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats dropDuplicates as a partitioning safety net; aggregation produces unique keys regardless of partitioning.

Option C: True only if quality is non-unique, which the next question rules out; without that assumption the diagnosis is correct, but it is not THE truth here.

Option D: Confuses the broadcast join's per-row behaviour with duplicate generation; the join is left-outer to a single-row-per-key reference.

fields.label: If the engineer can guarantee that quality has at most one row per (region, date), which edit eliminates the dropDuplicates shuffle (E3) without changing the output?
options: Add a broadcast hint on the quality DataFrame so Catalyst converts the SortMergeJoin to a BroadcastHashJoin and the post-join Exchange that drives dropDuplicates collapses into the hash on the broadcasted side of the join.

Replace dropDuplicates with a distinct call on the same columns so Catalyst recognises the equivalent semantics and merges the deduplication step into the HashAggregate that already runs above the join.

Replace dropDuplicates with a select of the keys plus the new column from quality, since the keys are already unique after the groupBy and the join with a unique-on-keys table cannot introduce duplicates.

Repartition the agg DataFrame on (region, date) before the join so the post-join Exchange is unnecessary, leaving the dropDuplicates step to run as a local operation on the already-partitioned output.
fields.correctAnswer: Replace dropDuplicates with a select of the keys plus the new column from quality, since the keys are already unique after the groupBy and the join with a unique-on-keys table cannot introduce duplicates.
fields.rationale:
If quality is unique on the join keys, the join cannot introduce duplicates and dropDuplicates is a no-op. Replacing it with a select that keeps the keys plus the new column eliminates the operator and its Exchange entirely. The broadcast hint changes the join strategy but does not by itself remove the dropDuplicates step. distinct and dropDuplicates compile to the same operator. Repartitioning before the join does not eliminate the post-join Exchange that the dropDuplicates currently introduces.

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer cannot guarantee uniqueness on quality, removing dropDuplicates risks emitting duplicates downstream and option A's broadcast hint becomes a partial fix that at least changes the join's shuffle pattern. The exercise's framing (uniqueness guarantee given) makes the removal safe.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Changes the join strategy but leaves dropDuplicates in place; the Exchange the dropDuplicates introduces remains.

Option B: Treats distinct as a different operator; Catalyst maps both to the same HashAggregate.

Option D: Repartitioning aligns the join's input but does not remove the post-join shuffle for the empty-functions aggregate.

fields.label: The plan also shows BroadcastExchange [B1] for the subs join. Why is this NOT counted as one of the shuffles?
options: BroadcastExchange copies the build side to every executor as a single transfer, which uses the network but does not redistribute the probe-side data and therefore does not match the cost profile that motivates counting shuffles.

BroadcastExchange runs only when the build-side table is small enough that Catalyst can materialise it in driver memory, and the resulting transfer is local enough that the engine excludes it from the shuffle metrics.

BroadcastExchange uses a different physical plan operator that does not write shuffle data to disk, and the count of shuffles in the SQL UI is based on the number of disk writes the engine produces during the run.

BroadcastExchange in this plan applies to the substations reference table, which is small and read once; the cost is amortised across the run and Spark counts only data-volume-driven exchanges as shuffles.
fields.correctAnswer: BroadcastExchange copies the build side to every executor as a single transfer, which uses the network but does not redistribute the probe-side data and therefore does not match the cost profile that motivates counting shuffles.
fields.rationale:
Broadcast and shuffle are different distributions. Broadcast sends the small build side to every executor once. Shuffle redistributes the probe-side rows across executors based on a key. Engineers count shuffles because their cost scales with the probe-side row count and the network bandwidth, which the broadcast does not consume in the same way. The other options invent specific exclusion mechanisms (driver memory, disk write counters, amortisation) that are not how Spark distinguishes the two.

When this answer is wrong: If the build-side table were not small (a large broadcast), the broadcast cost could exceed a shuffle's, and the engineer would treat it as a comparable concern. The exercise's framing (small substations table) makes the distinction clean.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a driver-memory criterion that decides classification; the criterion decides feasibility, not classification.

Option C: Bases the count on disk writes; broadcast does write spill on large broadcasts but the count is not what defines the term.

Option D: Reaches for amortisation reasoning; Spark's count is structural, not cost-amortised.
