tasks.title: When date Is Really a String

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing the Bronze schema for the meters feed that an upstream system produces. The schema declares date as a StringType because the source CSV had an inconsistent ISO-8601 format that a previous engineer normalised by reading it as a string. The downstream Silver pipeline filters by date and partitions output by date. A teammate raises a concern: the string-typed date column may be silently disabling optimisations that would otherwise speed up the consumers.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing the Bronze schema for the meters feed that an upstream system produces. The schema declares date as a StringType because the source CSV had an inconsistent ISO-8601 format that a previous engineer normalised by reading it as a string. The downstream Silver pipeline filters by date and partitions output by date. A teammate raises a concern: the string-typed date column may be silently disabling optimisations that would otherwise speed up the consumers.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: Three downstream pipelines filter the meters Bronze table by exact-day date. Each pipeline runs daily and reads only the most recent day in production, but historical reprocessing jobs occasionally request a date range, and the range scan performance has been degrading as the archive grows.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (currently with date stored as string '2026-03-15', candidate to convert to DateType)

evidence.title: Current Schema
evidence.content:
root
 |-- meter_id: string (nullable = false)
 |-- date: string (nullable = false)
 |-- daily_kw: double (nullable = true)
 |-- region: string (nullable = false)
 |-- customer_type: string (nullable = true)
 |-- substation_id: string (nullable = false)

evidence.title: Current Partitioning
evidence.content: partitionBy('date'): each daily run writes to /bronze/meters/date=2026-03-15/...

evidence.label: Consumer Query Patterns
evidence.content:
[
  "Daily run: filter where date = '2026-03-15'",
  "Backfill: filter where date between '2026-03-01' and '2026-03-31'",
  "Audit: filter where date >= '2025-01-01' and date < '2026-01-01'"
]

evidence.title: Candidate Change
evidence.content: Cast date to DateType at the Bronze ingestion step and re-partition the table by the typed date column.

fields.label: Which optimisation does the string-typed date most directly inhibit when the consumer issues a range filter?
options: Catalyst cannot apply the partition filter to a string column because the partition scheme requires a typed column to match the directory naming convention used during writes to the lakehouse layer.

The Parquet reader cannot use the column index for date when the column is stored as a string; the index is only built for typed columns and pruning per row group falls back to a full scan in the query.

Range comparison on string values follows lexicographic ordering, which lines up with ISO-8601 dates for fully formatted strings but offers Catalyst no semantic-date pruning that a typed column would enable.

The schema inference step rejects mixed-format date strings as invalid and Spark falls back to reading every directory because the partition filter cannot resolve the predicate against the inferred column.
fields.correctAnswer: Range comparison on string values follows lexicographic ordering, which lines up with ISO-8601 dates for fully formatted strings but offers Catalyst no semantic-date pruning that a typed column would enable.
fields.rationale:
The most direct issue is range comparison semantics. ISO-8601 strings happen to sort lexicographically the same way dates sort, so a string range filter still returns the right rows; what is missing is the date-typed partition pruning that lets Catalyst bound the scan by an interval. The first option's claim that partition filters reject string columns is wrong (they work fine). The second confuses Parquet's column index with the partition pruning layer. The fourth invents a schema-inference rejection that does not happen.

When this answer is wrong: If the upstream date strings used a non-ISO format like '03/15/2026', lexicographic ordering would no longer match calendar ordering and range filters could return wrong rows; the proximate concern would shift from optimisation to correctness. The exercise's framing (ISO-8601 strings) keeps the issue in the optimisation domain.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Asserts that partition pruning rejects string columns; it does not, the directory naming uses string-equivalent values regardless.

Option B: Conflates the Parquet column index (a row-group statistics structure) with the partition layer.

Option D: Invents an inference rejection step; Spark accepts heterogeneous strings without error.

fields.label: The teammate proposes casting date to DateType at ingestion. Which downstream behaviour changes the most because of this cast?
options: Range predicates on date become semantic comparisons that Catalyst can use to bound partition scans by interval, replacing the string comparisons with date-aware bounds at the planner step.
Equality predicates on date become faster because the typed column compares a 4-byte integer instead of a 10-character string at the executor row-by-row evaluation step.
Partition discovery skips type inference for the date directory names because Catalyst sees a typed schema and assigns the partition column its declared type without reading any file content.
Storage cost for the date column drops because DateType encodes as a single integer per row in Parquet whereas the string form encodes as a length-prefixed UTF-8 byte sequence per row.
fields.correctAnswer: Range predicates on date become semantic comparisons that Catalyst can use to bound partition scans by interval, replacing the string comparisons with date-aware bounds at the planner step.
fields.rationale:
Semantic range comparison on the partition column is the dominant downstream change. Catalyst can bound an interval like [2026-03-01, 2026-03-31] and prune partitions whose values fall outside it. Equality comparisons are already fast on strings (option B is a real but small effect). Partition discovery still infers types from directory names (option C overstates the change). Storage saving on the date column itself (option D) is real but not the primary downstream behaviour change.

When this answer is wrong: If the consumer queries are entirely equality-only (no range filters), option B's micro-improvement on equality comparison would be the dominant change. The exercise's framing (audit job runs ranges) makes the planner-level pruning the dominant gain.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names a real but small effect at the executor; the planner-level pruning gain is larger.

Option C: Overstates the partition discovery change; type inference still runs over directory names.

Option D: Names a real storage saving but it is the smallest of the three benefits.

fields.label: An engineer suggests skipping the cast and instead partitioning by a year_month derived column written alongside the date string. Which trade-off is the strongest argument against this proposal?
options: Adding a year_month column requires the daily ingestion job to compute and write a second column on every row, which increases the Bronze write throughput cost by a measurable amount across the year.

Day-level partition pruning is lost because partition filtering on year_month gives month-level granularity, and the daily-run consumers would scan the full month each day instead of one date directory.
The year_month column would require its own derivation logic during reads to map a date predicate to a year_month range, which complicates the consumer code beyond the original string-date pattern.
Range-spanning queries (the audit job covering a year) would still scan multiple year_month directories, so the proposal does not address the scenario the team brought up as the original concern.
fields.correctAnswer: Day-level partition pruning is lost because partition filtering on year_month gives month-level granularity, and the daily-run consumers would scan the full month each day instead of one date directory.
fields.rationale:
The proposal changes the partition granularity from day to month. Daily-run consumers would scan thirty directories of data instead of one to find the matching rows, which is exactly the cost the original concern wanted to fix. The other options name real but smaller costs (write throughput, predicate-mapping logic) or restate the original problem (range scans across the archive) rather than identifying the granularity loss as the binding cost.

When this answer is wrong: If the daily-run consumers were retired and only month-spanning audit jobs remained, the granularity loss would not matter and option D's range-scan cost would become the binding concern. The exercise's framing (three daily-run consumers) makes the granularity loss the primary trade-off.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names a real but minor cost at write time; the read-side granularity loss is the binding issue.

Option C: Treats consumer-side derivation logic as the binding cost; logic is cheap, the partition layout is what hurts.

Option D: Restates the original audit-job concern that the proposal does not address; a different complaint, not the strongest argument against the proposal.

fields.label: If the team adopts the DateType change, which existing piece of consumer code would still work unchanged after the cast?
options: A consumer that compares date to the literal string '2026-03-15' inside an expr() call would still work because expr accepts string-literal operands and Catalyst routes the comparison through the runtime expression engine.

A consumer that joins meters to a calendar table on date would still work because Spark casts both sides of an equality join to a common comparable type even when the join's source schemas declare different types.

A consumer that filters with col('date') == '2026-03-15' would still work because Spark performs implicit casts between StringType and DateType operands using the configured ANSI-compatibility setting at evaluation time.

A consumer that calls year(col('date')) would still work because the year function accepts both string and date operands and parses ISO-8601 strings with the same logic the cast applies during ingestion.
fields.correctAnswer: A consumer that calls year(col('date')) would still work because the year function accepts both string and date operands and parses ISO-8601 strings with the same logic the cast applies during ingestion.
fields.rationale:
Among the candidates, the only one that is safe under all common configurations is the call to the date-extracting helper, since it accepts both string ISO dates and a typed value without an implicit coercion. expr() with a string-literal comparison may or may not work depending on ANSI mode and is not guaranteed. Joins to a calendar table do require both sides to share a type after the cast and the join may fail with a type mismatch. col equality comparison between StringType and DateType triggers an implicit cast that is configuration-dependent and is not a safe assumption.

When this answer is wrong: If ANSI mode is disabled and implicit casts are allowed, option C's filter survives without code change because Spark casts the string literal to a date for comparison. The exercise's framing (no ANSI assumption) makes the year function the safe answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Trusts expr() to handle the cross-type comparison; behaviour is configuration-dependent.

Option B: Assumes Spark always coerces join keys; type mismatch on join keys raises a planning error in strict modes.

Option C: Relies on implicit-cast behaviour that depends on ANSI mode and is not portable.

fields.label: A reviewer asks why the team should do the cast at Bronze rather than at every Silver consumer. Which is the strongest argument for casting at Bronze?
options: Casting at Bronze runs once per ingestion and produces typed Parquet files that downstream consumers read directly, while casting at Silver runs once per consumer pipeline and pays the conversion cost across every read.

Casting at Bronze guarantees that every Silver consumer sees a consistent date type without relying on each pipeline to remember to apply the cast, removing a class of subtle correctness bugs from the schema-drift surface.

Casting at Bronze ensures the partition column is a typed value that participates in partition pruning across all consumers, while casting at Silver leaves the Bronze partition layer indexed by the original string form.

Casting at Bronze keeps the Bronze layer aligned with NordGrid's contract that Bronze stores raw bytes only after light type-and-format normalisation, which the team has already documented for the meters source schema.
fields.correctAnswer: Casting at Bronze ensures the partition column is a typed value that participates in partition pruning across all consumers, while casting at Silver leaves the Bronze partition layer indexed by the original string form.
fields.rationale:
The Bronze layer is the partition layer all consumers read from. If date stays a string at Bronze, every consumer's partition pruning runs against the string-typed partition column, even consumers that internally cast to date for their own predicates. Casting at Bronze is the only place the cast affects the partition layer that all consumers share. The other options name true facts (run-once cost, consistency, contract alignment) that are real benefits but secondary to the partition-layer effect.

When this answer is wrong: If the team's Bronze contract forbids any type changes and the partition layer is rebuilt by a separate Silver-layer process, casting at Silver would be the only viable choice and option D's contract argument would dominate. The exercise's framing (cast permitted at Bronze) makes the partition argument primary.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names the per-read cost as the binding argument; the partition layer is more impactful than the per-read CPU.

Option B: Names consistency as the binding argument; consistency is a benefit but the partition-layer behaviour is the structural one.

Option D: Reaches for the contract justification; true but secondary to the partition behaviour.

tasks.pssReference: Junior PS5 (Adding/Transforming Columns), Junior PS8 (Reading and Writing - schemas); Optimization Cross-Track OPT-J2 lessons 4-5, OPT-J3 lesson 6.

tasks.title: CSV, JSON, or Parquet for the New Source

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is wiring up a new feed that an upstream pricing service publishes as JSON Lines through an SFTP drop. The records hold tariff updates per customer_type per region per day, with about 20,000 rows landed each morning. Three downstream pipelines consume the feed: a Silver enrichment that joins it to meter readings, a quarterly audit job that scans a rolling 90-day window, and an ad-hoc analytics notebook that filters for one region and one customer_type. The team is debating whether to keep the Bronze layer as JSON, convert to CSV, or convert to Parquet at ingestion.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is wiring up a new feed that an upstream pricing service publishes as JSON Lines through an SFTP drop. The records hold tariff updates per customer_type per region per day, with about 20,000 rows landed each morning. Three downstream pipelines consume the feed: a Silver enrichment that joins it to meter readings, a quarterly audit job that scans a rolling 90-day window, and an ad-hoc analytics notebook that filters for one region and one customer_type. The team is debating whether to keep the Bronze layer as JSON, convert to CSV, or convert to Parquet at ingestion.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: All three downstream consumers run on the same Bronze table. The Silver enrichment runs daily and is the SLA-critical path; the audit job runs weekly; the analytics notebook is interactive. The Bronze format choice determines the read profile each consumer sees.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: tariffs.csv (4 rows, 2 columns) — used as a stand-in for the schema shape of the new feed

evidence.title: Feed Description
evidence.content: JSON Lines, ~20,000 rows/day, 8 fields (customer_type, region, date, price_per_kw, currency, version, valid_from, valid_to)

evidence.label: Consumer Query Patterns
evidence.content:
[
  "Silver enrichment: filter by date = today; project all 8 fields for join with meter readings",
  "Quarterly audit: filter by date between window_start and window_end (90 days); project customer_type, region, date, price_per_kw",
  "Analytics notebook: filter by region = 'NORTH' and customer_type = 'commercial'; project price_per_kw and valid_from"
]

evidence.label: Format Options
evidence.content:
[
  "Keep as JSON Lines at Bronze",
  "Convert to CSV at Bronze ingestion",
  "Convert to Parquet at Bronze ingestion (no partitioning)",
  "Convert to Parquet at Bronze ingestion partitioned by date"
]

fields.label: Which format choice gives all three consumers the strongest read-path optimisations?
options: Keeping the JSON Lines at Bronze preserves the structure the upstream service emits and lets each consumer pick the columns it cares about during the read step without a conversion stage in between.
Converting to CSV at Bronze ingestion is the cheapest move because every consumer can use Spark's CSV reader without an extra schema declaration step on the Bronze table after the daily load.

Converting to Parquet at Bronze ingestion without partitioning gives consumers columnar reads and predicate pushdown on the eight fields, including the column pruning the analytics notebook benefits from on its read.

Converting to Parquet at Bronze ingestion partitioned by date adds directory-level pruning to the columnar reads, which the Silver enrichment and the quarterly audit both use through their date predicates on every read.
fields.correctAnswer: Converting to Parquet at Bronze ingestion partitioned by date adds directory-level pruning to the columnar reads, which the Silver enrichment and the quarterly audit both use through their date predicates on every read.
fields.rationale:
The audit and the daily enrichment both predicate on date, which makes the directory-pruning layer worth the partition cost. All three consumers benefit from columnar reads: the analytics notebook's two-field projection out of eight is a 75% column read reduction, and the audit's four-field projection saves half. The unpartitioned-Parquet option (C) misses the directory pruning. JSON and CSV give neither.

When this answer is wrong: If none of the consumers filtered by date and all three issued ad-hoc filters on different fields, partitioning by date would add overhead without payoff and option C (unpartitioned Parquet) would be the right move. The exercise's framing (two of three filter by date) makes the partitioned form the strongest choice.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats format choice as a transparency issue; the read-path losses against Parquet outweigh any conversion cost.

Option B: Picks CSV for its simplicity but misses that CSV gives away the same columnar and partition optimisations as JSON.

Option C: Stops at columnar reads without considering that two consumers filter by date and would benefit from directory pruning.

fields.label: The team considers keeping the JSON form unchanged. Which read-path optimisation is most directly lost relative to Parquet?
options: Schema inference on JSON requires a full pre-scan of the data on the first read, which adds a constant overhead to the Silver enrichment that the team would have to amortise across the daily window of records.
Column-level reads do not exist for JSON because JSON is a row-oriented format; every consumer reads every field of every record even when the projection asks for only two fields out of the eight.

JSON Lines does not support partition pruning at the directory level because the format does not declare how the data is partitioned, so the consumer has to scan every file in the table on every read.

JSON Lines records cannot carry typed columns because the format encodes everything as text, so predicate pushdown requires Spark to materialise each field as a string before any comparison happens at the scan step.
fields.correctAnswer: Column-level reads do not exist for JSON because JSON is a row-oriented format; every consumer reads every field of every record even when the projection asks for only two fields out of the eight.
fields.rationale:
The dominant loss against Parquet is per-column reads. JSON's row layout forces the reader to materialise all eight fields on every read, even when the projection asks for two; the 75% column-read saving the analytics notebook would get from Parquet is unavailable on JSON. Schema inference cost (option A) is real but only on first read and avoidable with a declared schema. JSON does support partition pruning at the directory level when written under a partitioned layout (option C is wrong on that). JSON's text encoding does add per-field parsing cost but predicate pushdown semantics are not the dominant gap.

When this answer is wrong: If all three consumers projected every field on every read (no projection narrowing), the column-read advantage of Parquet would not matter and option A's schema-inference cost would become the most concrete loss. The exercise's framing (consumers project subsets) makes the column-read gap dominant.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names the schema-inference cost as the dominant loss; it is real but one-time per workflow.

Option C: Asserts JSON cannot be partitioned; partitioned-by-date JSON is supported, just rarely useful.

Option D: Confuses text encoding with predicate pushdown semantics; Parquet's pushdown is statistics-based, not type-based.

fields.label: An engineer asks why CSV is not on the table as the right move for this feed, given how cheap CSV is to read. Which response best explains the gap?
options: CSV pays the same row-oriented read cost as JSON without giving back the columnar reads or per-row-group statistics that the analytics notebook needs to filter by region efficiently across the daily files.

CSV requires the engineer to declare a schema explicitly because the format does not encode types, and the schema declaration step adds a maintenance burden on the Bronze layer that JSON avoids by keeping the type tags.

CSV cannot represent the nested structure that the upstream service publishes alongside the flat fields, and converting to CSV would require flattening the records during ingestion at the cost of the data shape.

CSV's schema-on-read pattern conflicts with the schema-on-write contract that NordGrid uses for the Bronze layer, and adopting CSV here would create an exception that the team has to document for each consumer.
fields.correctAnswer: CSV pays the same row-oriented read cost as JSON without giving back the columnar reads or per-row-group statistics that the analytics notebook needs to filter by region efficiently across the daily files.
fields.rationale:
CSV and JSON share the row-oriented limitation: every consumer pays the same per-row read cost regardless of how many fields it needs. The columnar advantage and the row-group statistics that Parquet adds are exactly what the analytics notebook (and the audit) wants. Schema declaration cost (option B) is a real but minor friction, the upstream emits flat records (option C is not relevant), and the schema-on-write contract argument (option D) is a process answer rather than a performance one.

When this answer is wrong: If the team's ingestion infrastructure supports only CSV/JSON (a real constraint at some shops), the choice between the two would come down to schema-declaration cost and option B's argument would dominate. The exercise's framing (Parquet is on the table) makes the columnar gap the relevant point.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats schema declaration as the binding cost; declaration is one-time per schema, not a per-read cost.

Option C: Invents a flattening problem the feed does not have; the upstream emits flat fields.

Option D: Names a process argument instead of a performance one; the question is about read-path performance.

fields.label: The team picks Parquet partitioned by date. Which downstream consumer benefits the LEAST from the date-partition choice (relative to unpartitioned Parquet)?
options: The Silver enrichment benefits least because it reads only one day per run and the directory structure adds a discovery step on each run, paying a small overhead that does not show up for the audit job.

The quarterly audit benefits least because the rolling 90-day window scans a hundred or so files regardless of the partition layout, and the directory pruning saves only a few percent of the read at that window size.

The analytics notebook benefits least because its filters are on region and customer_type rather than on date, and the date partitioning has no effect on a query that does not include a date predicate at the filter step.

All three consumers benefit equally because each consumer has at least one date-based predicate in its query path, and the directory pruning fires uniformly across all three consumers' read patterns on every run.
fields.correctAnswer: The analytics notebook benefits least because its filters are on region and customer_type rather than on date, and the date partitioning has no effect on a query that does not include a date predicate at the filter step.
fields.rationale:
Date-partitioning helps queries that have a date predicate. The analytics notebook filters by region and customer_type only — no date — so the partition layer cannot prune anything for this query. The notebook still benefits from columnar reads, but those come from Parquet, not from the partitioning choice. The Silver enrichment uses date heavily (option A is the wrong direction), the audit also benefits from windowed pruning (option B understates the saving), and option D claims uniform benefit, which the analytics notebook contradicts.

When this answer is wrong: If the analytics notebook were updated to scope its queries to a recent date range (say, last 30 days), it would benefit from partitioning too and option B's audit-job argument would be the strongest. The exercise's framing (notebook does not filter by date) makes the notebook the least beneficiary.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inverts the benefit; the daily run gains the most from one-day directory pruning.

Option B: Understates the audit's saving; pruning a year archive to a 90-day window is roughly 25% read versus full scan.

Option D: Asserts uniform benefit; the analytics notebook query has no date predicate and prunes nothing.

tasks.pssReference: Junior PS8 (Reading and Writing - file formats, partition discovery); Optimization Cross-Track OPT-J3 lessons 1, 3-4.

tasks.title: Partition by region or by meter_id

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is writing a new Silver table that holds enriched per-meter daily readings. The team is deciding which column to use as the write-side partition. The candidates are region (cardinality 4), meter_id (cardinality 500,000), date (cardinality grows over time, currently ~1,000 days in the archive), and customer_type (cardinality 4). The engineer drafts a write spec partitioned by meter_id, runs a small backfill, and notices the output directory contains hundreds of thousands of subdirectories. The lead asks the engineer to step back and pick a different partition column.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is writing a new Silver table that holds enriched per-meter daily readings. The team is deciding which column to use as the write-side partition. The candidates are region (cardinality 4), meter_id (cardinality 500,000), date (cardinality grows over time, currently ~1,000 days in the archive), and customer_type (cardinality 4). The engineer drafts a write spec partitioned by meter_id, runs a small backfill, and notices the output directory contains hundreds of thousands of subdirectories. The lead asks the engineer to step back and pick a different partition column.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver table is read by four consumer pipelines daily and is rebuilt monthly from a 90-day rolling window of Bronze data. Every read of the table benefits from partition pruning when the consumer filters on the partition column. The write-side cost grows with the number of partition directories the writer creates.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (20 rows, 6 columns; columns include meter_id, region, date, customer_type, substation_id)

evidence.title: Write Spec Proposed
evidence.content: df.write.partitionBy('meter_id').mode('overwrite').parquet('s3://nordgrid/silver/meters_enriched/')

evidence.label: Cardinality Summary
evidence.content:
{
  "meter_id": "500,000 distinct values",
  "region": "4 distinct values (NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST)",
  "date": "~1,000 distinct values across the archive",
  "customer_type": "4 distinct values (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural)",
  "substation_id": "200 distinct values"
}

evidence.label: Consumer Query Patterns
evidence.content:
[
  "Daily run pipeline: filter by date = today, project all columns",
  "Regional billing report: filter by region = ?, group by date",
  "Audit job: filter by date between window_start and window_end",
  "Substation capacity report: filter by substation_id IN (small list)"
]

evidence.title: Data Volume
evidence.content: Silver table: ~3GB per day, ~270GB across 90-day rolling window

fields.label: Why is meter_id a poor partition column for this table despite being a unique identifier?
options: Cardinality is too high relative to the data volume; partitioning by meter_id creates 500,000 directories with about 6KB per file each, which the file system handles slowly and which gives no consumer a useful pruning predicate.

Partitioning by meter_id requires the writer to sort the entire DataFrame on the meter_id column before producing the partition directories, and the sort cost dominates the write step on the 90-day rolling window data load.

Partitioning by meter_id forces the read step to perform a directory listing across all 500,000 directories on every consumer pipeline run, even when the predicate filters on a different column entirely.
Partitioning by meter_id breaks the join with substations because the partition column is on the wrong side of the join and Spark cannot use a partition-aware join strategy with that layout choice.
fields.correctAnswer: Cardinality is too high relative to the data volume; partitioning by meter_id creates 500,000 directories with about 6KB per file each, which the file system handles slowly and which gives no consumer a useful pruning predicate.
fields.rationale:
Partition cardinality should match the access pattern and the data volume. meter_id is unique, so partitioning by it produces one directory per meter. Average file size becomes about 6KB on a 3GB-per-day load split 500,000 ways. None of the consumer queries even filter on meter_id, so the layout does not help any pruning either. The other options invent specific failure modes (forced sort, listing across all directories, broken joins) that are not the proximate problem.

When this answer is wrong: If the table were a long-running per-meter event log where every read is keyed on a single meter_id, the access-pattern half of the argument would not apply and the file-size half would still hurt; the answer would still flag the layout as wrong but for a narrower reason. The exercise's framing (no consumer filters on meter_id) makes both halves apply.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Asserts a forced sort that partitionBy does not require; partition writers shuffle by key but do not full-sort.

Option C: Overstates directory listing; partitioned reads list directories matching the predicate, not all of them.

Option D: Invents a join-strategy interaction that partitioning does not have at this layer.

fields.label: Looking at the consumer query patterns, which column is the strongest single-column partition choice?
options: region is the strongest single-column choice because three of the four consumers filter on region directly or indirectly through their predicate, and the four-way split keeps the directory count manageable for the writer.

date is the strongest single-column choice because the daily run filters on it directly and the audit filters on it as a range; the two date-based consumers are the most performance-sensitive of the four pipelines.

substation_id is the strongest single-column choice because the substation capacity report filters by substation_id IN a list and the partition layer can prune the directories that match the list members on every read.

customer_type is the strongest single-column choice because the four-way split mirrors the region split's directory count, and customer_type aligns with the regional billing report's grouping behaviour.
fields.correctAnswer: date is the strongest single-column choice because the daily run filters on it directly and the audit filters on it as a range; the two date-based consumers are the most performance-sensitive of the four pipelines.
fields.rationale:
Among the four consumer queries, two predicate on the date column (one as equality on today, one as a window) and those two pipelines are the most volume-critical of the set. region as a partition key (option A) helps the regional billing report but only one of the four consumers, and the daily run scans every region directory. Cardinality on date is high but bounded by retention; the writer creates one new directory per day, which is a normal operational pattern.

When this answer is wrong: If the regional billing report ran multiple times per hour and dwarfed the daily-run cost in cluster time, region would become the strongest choice because pruning saves a constant 75% on every report run. The exercise's framing (single daily run plus weekly/audit pattern) makes date the dominant axis.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks region for matching one consumer's predicate; the date-using consumers are higher-volume and more SLA-critical.

Option C: Picks substation_id for matching one consumer; 200 directories is workable but only one consumer prunes on it.

Option D: Picks customer_type for matching the directory count of region; no consumer filters on customer_type.

fields.label: The lead suggests two-level partitioning: 'region' followed by 'date'. Which downside of this layout is the strongest argument against it?
options: The two-level layout doubles the partition discovery cost because Spark lists region directories first and then lists each region's date directories, multiplying the metadata calls the planner makes on every read.

The two-level layout encodes region in the directory path before date, which means filters on date alone can no longer benefit from partition pruning because the filter has to traverse the region layer first to reach the dates.

The two-level layout creates roughly 4 × 1,000 directories across the 90-day rolling window, which scales linearly with the archive growth and creates a directory-count problem when the archive extends beyond a few years.

The two-level layout produces around 4 × 90 directories on the rolling window, which the writer maintains cleanly, but each per-day-per-region directory holds about 7MB and creates a small-files problem at read time on each daily run.
fields.correctAnswer: The two-level layout produces around 4 × 90 directories on the rolling window, which the writer maintains cleanly, but each per-day-per-region directory holds about 7MB and creates a small-files problem at read time on each daily run.
fields.rationale:
At 3GB total daily volume split across the layered keys, each leaf directory ends up around 188MB raw and roughly 7MB compressed in Parquet. That is small enough to start running into the small-files cost on read. The other options name effects that are real but smaller (extra metadata calls, archive-growth-driven directory counts) or invert the truth (filters on date alone do still prune even with a higher-level region directory).

When this answer is wrong: If the daily volume were 30GB instead of 3GB, each per-day-per-region directory would hold 75MB compressed and the small-files cost would not apply; option C's archive-growth concern would then become the dominant trade-off. The exercise's framing (3GB/day) puts the small-files cost in the binding range.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Claims doubled discovery cost; the cost is metadata, not double, and is small on most stores.

Option B: Asserts that two-level partitioning blocks date-alone pruning; it does not, Spark prunes on any prefix or any subset of the layered keys.

Option C: Names the right scaling law but sets the threshold higher than the small-files cost; small-files hurts first.

fields.label: If the team wants per-meter access to be fast (e.g., for a customer service workflow that fetches all readings for one meter), which mechanism is the right tool?
options: A secondary write with the same data partitioned by meter_id at coarser bins (e.g., the first two characters of meter_id) gives 256 directories instead of 500,000, balancing per-meter access speed and directory count.

A bucketing layout on meter_id (with bucketBy at write time) gives shuffle-free joins on meter_id without producing one directory per value, which is the right tool for per-key access at this cardinality.
A Z-ordering on meter_id within the date-partitioned layout gives data skipping on meter_id without paying the 500,000-directory cost, and works well for selective per-meter lookups on Delta tables.

A separate index file alongside the date-partitioned Parquet listing the meter_id ranges per file gives the customer service workflow a way to look up the right files without partitioning the table by meter_id at all.
fields.correctAnswer: A Z-ordering on meter_id within the date-partitioned layout gives data skipping on meter_id without paying the 500,000-directory cost, and works well for selective per-meter lookups on Delta tables.
fields.rationale:
Delta's clustering layer organises rows within a partition file so that values close on the chosen key sit next to one another; combined with file-level statistics, Spark skips entire files when the predicate is selective on that key. This gives per-key fast access without the directory cost. Bucketing (option B) helps shuffle-free joins but does not give the directory-listing-free per-key lookup the customer service workflow wants. Coarse-bin partitioning (option A) is a workaround. A side index (option D) is custom infrastructure rather than a Spark mechanism.

When this answer is wrong: If the table were stored as plain Parquet (not Delta), Z-ordering would not be available and bucketing or coarse-bin partitioning would be the right tools; the exercise's framing (Delta is on the table for the senior level but mentioned here as the right tool when available) keeps Z-order the right answer when the engineer can choose Delta.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reaches for a coarse-bin workaround; works but is a fallback, not the right tool when Z-order is available.

Option B: Picks bucketing for any per-key need; bucketing optimises joins, not point lookups.

Option D: Invents custom indexing infrastructure; standard Spark/Delta features cover the case.

fields.label: After picking date as the partition column, the engineer notices the daily run still benefits but the regional billing report does not. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The regional billing report filters by region rather than by date, so the date partition provides no pruning for that consumer; the report still benefits from the columnar reads but pays full directory listing on each run.

The regional billing report's groupBy on date forces a shuffle that defeats the partition layout because the grouping key is the partition column, which Catalyst handles by repartitioning at the aggregate boundary on every run.

The regional billing report's filter on region is supposed to be expressed as a date range that bounds the region's reporting window, and the filter form chosen by the engineer is what blocks the partition pruning at the planner step.

The regional billing report's read does benefit from date partitioning at the write side because the read engine still skips rolled-back days, but the runtime metric the engineer is reading does not surface this saving in the daily summary view.
fields.correctAnswer: The regional billing report filters by region rather than by date, so the date partition provides no pruning for that consumer; the report still benefits from the columnar reads but pays full directory listing on each run.
fields.rationale:
Partition pruning helps only when the consumer's predicate references the partition column. The regional billing report filters by region, not by date, so the date partition does not prune anything for it. The report still gets columnar reads from Parquet but reads every date directory the table has. The other options invent shuffle effects, predicate-form requirements, or runtime-metric-display issues that do not match the consumer pattern.

When this answer is wrong: If the regional billing report were rewritten to scope its query to a date window (e.g., last month's report runs on last month's data), it would benefit from date partitioning too. The exercise's framing (filter by region, no date scope) keeps the pruning gap.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Reaches for a shuffle-defeats-partition story that does not apply; aggregate shuffles are unrelated to read-side pruning.

Option C: Asserts that the report's filter form is what blocks pruning; the report has no date predicate to block at all.

Option D: Invents a metric-display-bug explanation; the saving simply does not exist for this query pattern.

tasks.title: The 24,000 Tiny Files

description.context: A NordGrid engineer inherits the Silver meters table. The pipeline that produces it runs every 30 minutes during the day and writes a small batch each time. The output directory now contains 24,000 Parquet files spread across about 1,000 date subdirectories, with most files sized between 200KB and 800KB. Downstream readers complain that scans on this table take three to four times longer than scans on a comparable table that the same team rebuilt last quarter. The engineer is asked to pick a remedy from a set of proposals.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer inherits the Silver meters table. The pipeline that produces it runs every 30 minutes during the day and writes a small batch each time. The output directory now contains 24,000 Parquet files spread across about 1,000 date subdirectories, with most files sized between 200KB and 800KB. Downstream readers complain that scans on this table take three to four times longer than scans on a comparable table that the same team rebuilt last quarter. The engineer is asked to pick a remedy from a set of proposals.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver table is read by the daily Gold aggregator, two analytics notebooks, and a quarterly audit. The audit reads the full archive and is the most affected: the listing step alone (resolving 24,000 file paths from object storage) takes longer than the actual data scan once it begins.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Silver layer is partitioned by date, written incrementally every 30 minutes)

evidence.title: Current Layout
evidence.content: s3://nordgrid/silver/meters/date=YYYY-MM-DD/part-00000-...parquet (one or more part files per 30-minute write, up to ~24 per day per writer instance)

evidence.title: File Size Distribution
evidence.content: p50: 480KB, p90: 720KB, p99: 1.4MB. Total table size: ~14GB across 24,000 files.

evidence.title: Incremental Write Pattern
evidence.content: Each 30-minute batch appends a small partition write (1-3 files) into the current date directory.

evidence.label: Candidate Remedies
evidence.content:
[
  "Repartition the DataFrame to 1 partition before each write so the writer produces one file per write call",
  "Coalesce the DataFrame to a target number of partitions before each write to limit file count per batch",
  "Raise spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile so the writer combines incoming rows into fewer larger files",
  "Run a separate compaction job nightly that rewrites each date directory as a small number of larger files"
]

fields.label: Why do 24,000 small files cost more on read than 1,000 medium-to-large files holding the same data?
options: Each file open requires a separate task in the cluster's scheduler, and 24,000 tasks introduce coordination overhead that grows non-linearly when tasks finish faster than the driver can dispatch the next ones at scale.

Each file open issues a metadata round-trip to object storage and parses the Parquet footer; these costs are largely per-file rather than per-byte and dominate the scan when files sit well below the read-block size.

Small files miss the read-buffer pool because the Parquet reader caches whole files in memory, so 24,000 files pressure the buffer pool harder than 1,000 files that fit comfortably in the cache during a scan.

Small files break the columnar layout because each file holds too few rows for the row-group structure to populate column statistics, which the planner uses for pruning at the scan operator level on every read.
fields.correctAnswer: Each file open issues a metadata round-trip to object storage and parses the Parquet footer; these costs are largely per-file rather than per-byte and dominate the scan when files sit well below the read-block size.
fields.rationale:
Storage round-trips and footer parses are paid once per file regardless of size. With files at 480KB median, those fixed costs dominate the actual data read time. Scheduler overhead from 24,000 tasks (option A) is real but smaller than the per-file I/O cost on object storage. The buffer-pool framing in option C is wrong (Parquet does not cache whole files). The columnar-layout argument in option D is wrong at this scale: even small files have valid statistics, just amortised over fewer rows.

When this answer is wrong: If the small files were on a fast local disk (not object storage), the per-file overhead would be much smaller and the cost might be dominated by something else (e.g., scheduler overhead from many tasks). The exercise's framing (object storage) makes the metadata round-trip the binding cost.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names scheduler coordination as the dominant cost; it contributes but is much smaller than the per-file I/O on object storage.

Option C: Invents a buffer-pool caching mechanism that the Parquet reader does not implement.

Option D: Asserts that small files break columnar statistics; statistics are populated at the row-group level, which works at small scales too.

fields.label: Which proposed remedy addresses the root cause without introducing a new problem on the write path?
options: Repartitioning to 1 partition per write produces one file per write call but funnels the entire 30-minute batch through a single executor, which makes the write step a serial bottleneck on every batch.

Coalescing to a small target number of partitions limits the file count per batch but produces fewer files per write than the cluster could in parallel, leaving a fraction of the file count problem in place across days.

Raising spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile lets the writer combine more rows per file at write time, but the 30-minute batch only produces enough rows for a single small file already, so the threshold does not change file count.

A nightly compaction job rewrites each date directory as a few larger files, leaving the 30-minute write path untouched and addressing the historical small-file accumulation that the readers hit during the audit run.
fields.correctAnswer: A nightly compaction job rewrites each date directory as a few larger files, leaving the 30-minute write path untouched and addressing the historical small-file accumulation that the readers hit during the audit run.
fields.rationale:
Compaction targets the accumulated state of historical files without coupling to the write path. The 30-minute writes continue producing one or two small files per batch, and a nightly job rewrites each completed day's directory into a few larger files. Repartition-to-1 (option A) serialises the writer. Coalesce (option B) is a partial fix that still leaves multiple small files per batch. maxRecordsPerFile (option C) does not combine small batches; it only splits large output partitions.

When this answer is wrong: If the 30-minute writes produced enough rows that maxRecordsPerFile could meaningfully bin them at write time, option C would directly fix the problem at the source. The exercise's framing (small per-batch row count) makes the write-time threshold inert.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks single-partition write for predictable file count; pays a serial-write cost on every batch.

Option B: Picks coalesce as a middle ground; still leaves the small-files problem partly in place.

Option C: Misreads maxRecordsPerFile as a lower-bound combiner; it is an upper-bound splitter.

fields.label: After the compaction job runs for a week, the engineer notices that today's date directory still has 48 small files. Why?
options: The compaction job runs nightly and the current day's directory has not yet been compacted; today's files will be merged when tonight's job runs against the previous day's directory after the daily roll boundary.

The compaction job is configured to skip the current day's directory because compacting an actively-written directory risks lock contention with the 30-minute writer's appends; only closed-day directories are compacted on each job run.

The compaction job skips files smaller than its target file size because rewriting them costs more than the read saving they provide; today's files have not yet accumulated to the size threshold the job uses.
The compaction job compacts only files whose modification time is older than a configured age; today's files were written within the age window and are excluded from the current job run by design.
fields.correctAnswer: The compaction job is configured to skip the current day's directory because compacting an actively-written directory risks lock contention with the 30-minute writer's appends; only closed-day directories are compacted on each job run.
fields.rationale:
Compacting a directory that is being actively appended risks file-handle lock contention with the writer; the safe pattern is to compact yesterday's directory after the daily roll, leaving today's directory alone. Option A states the same outcome but credits scheduling rather than safety. Option C invents a size-threshold rule that the typical compaction job does not have. Option D invents an age-based exclusion that is neither standard nor accurate.

When this answer is wrong: If the table were stored as Delta (where snapshot isolation makes compaction concurrency-safe), the same-day compaction would be safe and option A's scheduling-only diagnosis would apply. The exercise's framing (plain Parquet) makes the safety reason primary.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names the correct visible behaviour but credits scheduling rather than the safety reason behind the schedule.

Option C: Invents a per-file size threshold; the directory-level compaction does not work this way.

Option D: Invents an age-based rule that is not part of the standard compaction pattern.

fields.label: An engineer asks whether maxRecordsPerFile is the right setting to manage going forward. Which statement is correct about its role?
options: maxRecordsPerFile sets an upper bound on the number of records per file at write time, splitting large output partitions into multiple files; it does not combine small batches into larger files at the write step.

maxRecordsPerFile sets a target number of records per file that the writer aims for, combining small input batches into larger output files when the target is set above the per-batch row count at write time.

maxRecordsPerFile sets a soft target that the writer respects when the cluster has spare capacity but ignores when the executor pool is saturated, leading to inconsistent file sizes across batches in production.
maxRecordsPerFile sets the row-group size inside each Parquet file, so raising it produces fewer row groups per file rather than fewer files per batch in the write output.
fields.correctAnswer: maxRecordsPerFile sets an upper bound on the number of records per file at write time, splitting large output partitions into multiple files; it does not combine small batches into larger files at the write step.
fields.rationale:
maxRecordsPerFile is an upper bound the writer respects when an output partition would otherwise produce a single very large file. It splits large outputs into multiple files of at most that many records each. It does not combine small batches into larger files; combining requires either fewer partitions on the input DataFrame or a separate compaction step. The other options misread its role (combiner, soft target, row-group size).

When this answer is wrong: If the engineer were writing a single large Gold table with millions of rows in one batch, maxRecordsPerFile would be the right tool to limit per-file size. The exercise's framing (small frequent batches) makes the combiner role what is missing, which the setting does not provide.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Inverts the role; maxRecordsPerFile is a splitter, not a combiner.

Option C: Adds a soft-vs-hard distinction that does not exist; the setting is a hard upper bound.

Option D: Confuses file-level setting with row-group-level setting; row-group size is a different option.

fields.label: The engineer ships compaction. Six months later, the audit job still reads more files than the engineer expected. Which check is the right next step?
options: Read the compaction job's run log to confirm it has been running on schedule and check for partitions it skipped or failed to compact, since long-running compaction setups can silently miss days when the underlying job fails partially.

Inspect the per-partition file count on the Silver directory, since incremental writes between compactions accumulate small files and the file count steady state depends on the compaction-run-to-write-frequency ratio.

Re-run the compaction job manually on the current month to confirm it produces the expected file count, then compare against historical compactions to see whether the job's behaviour has drifted across its operational lifetime.

Profile the audit job's listing step in the Spark UI to see how much time goes to listing versus reading, and use the ratio to decide whether the file count is the binding cost or whether another step in the audit is the slow part.
fields.correctAnswer: Inspect the per-partition file count on the Silver directory, since incremental writes between compactions accumulate small files and the file count steady state depends on the compaction-run-to-write-frequency ratio.
fields.rationale:
Confirm the symptom directly: count how many files each date directory currently holds. Compaction sets a steady state file count that depends on how often the job runs versus how often new files are added between runs; the file count drift is what readers feel. Reading the compaction log (option A) is fine but is a downstream check after the count itself shows a problem. Manual re-run (option C) is reactive. Listing-versus-reading profile (option D) is useful but assumes the file count is already known.

When this answer is wrong: If the file count looks sane but reads are still slow, profiling listing-versus-reading (option D) becomes the right next step because the file count is no longer the binding cost. The exercise's framing (audit reads more files than expected) makes the file count the first thing to check.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Goes to the run log without first confirming the count; the log is one cause of count drift, not the only one.

Option C: Runs compaction manually as a diagnosis; that is a fix, not a check.

Option D: Profiles upstream from the count; useful but the count check is more direct.

tasks.title: The Regex UDF That Could Be a Function

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver pipeline that runs in 14 minutes. Profiling shows that 9 of those minutes are spent inside a Python UDF that extracts a four-character station code from each meter_id. Every meter_id has the form 'MTR-WXYZ-12345678' where WXYZ is the station code. The UDF compiles a regex once at module load and applies it row by row. The team's lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements and pick the one that preserves the semantics with the largest performance gain.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver pipeline that runs in 14 minutes. Profiling shows that 9 of those minutes are spent inside a Python UDF that extracts a four-character station code from each meter_id. Every meter_id has the form 'MTR-WXYZ-12345678' where WXYZ is the station code. The UDF compiles a regex once at module load and applies it row by row. The team's lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements and pick the one that preserves the semantics with the largest performance gain.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver pipeline runs every 30 minutes and feeds three downstream consumers. Cutting the 9-minute UDF segment to under 1 minute would bring total pipeline time from 14 minutes back under the 7-minute target the team set when the pipeline was first written.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (meter_id format 'MTR-WXYZ-12345678'; station code is positions 5-8 inclusive, zero-indexed; about 500,000 rows per daily Silver run)

evidence.label: Udf Implementation
evidence.content:
import re
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import StringType

_pattern = re.compile(r'^MTR-([A-Z]{4})-\d{8}$')

@udf(returnType=StringType())
def extract_station_code(meter_id):
    if meter_id is None:
        return None
    m = _pattern.match(meter_id)
    return m.group(1) if m else None

df = df.withColumn('station_code', extract_station_code('meter_id'))

evidence.label: Candidate Replacements
evidence.content:
[
  "regexp_extract(col('meter_id'), r'^MTR-([A-Z]{4})-\\d{8}$', 1)",
  "substring(col('meter_id'), 5, 4) — positional substring, 1-indexed",
  "split(col('meter_id'), '-').getItem(1)",
  "A different UDF written in Pandas with @pandas_udf for vectorised execution"
]

fields.label: Why does the existing UDF take 9 of the pipeline's 14 minutes despite the precompiled regex?
options: The regex match itself is the expensive step because Python's re module backtracks on each row, and 500,000 rows of backtracking accumulate to the 9 minutes the engineer observes in the profiler.

The UDF allocates a fresh Python string object for the matched group on each row, and the garbage collection that runs across 500,000 allocated objects is what the profiler reports as the bulk of the UDF time.
The UDF holds the Python global interpreter lock for the regex evaluation, which serialises across executor cores and pushes the parallel pipeline into a serial section that lasts 9 minutes.

Each UDF call serialises the row to Python, runs the regex, and serialises the result back to the JVM; the per-row Python boundary crossing is what dominates and is independent of how the regex itself is implemented.
fields.correctAnswer: Each UDF call serialises the row to Python, runs the regex, and serialises the result back to the JVM; the per-row Python boundary crossing is what dominates and is independent of how the regex itself is implemented.
fields.rationale:
Spark UDFs that take Python functions cross the language boundary on every row. Each call serialises the row's value, sends it to the Python worker, runs the UDF, and sends the result back. The cost is proportional to the row count and largely independent of what the Python code does. The regex itself is a small fraction of the per-row time; backtracking, GIL, and GC explanations are the wrong layer.

When this answer is wrong: If the UDF were doing genuinely heavy Python work per row (e.g., a model inference), the Python computation could rival the boundary cost and option A's framing would be a partial truth. The exercise's framing (precompiled regex on a short string) makes the boundary the dominant cost.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Pins the cost on regex backtracking; for this pattern there is no backtracking and the regex itself is fast.

Option B: Reaches for GC pressure as the dominant cost; allocations exist but are not 9 of 14 minutes.

Option C: Invokes the GIL for executor parallelism; the Python workers are separate processes and the GIL is per-worker, not a serialiser.

fields.label: Which of the four candidates is the right replacement?
options: The split-then-getItem approach is the right replacement because it expresses the same string operation in a structural way that the planner can apply column-wise without per-row Python work in the executor.

The regexp_extract built-in is the right replacement because it expresses the same regex pattern at the Catalyst level, runs in the JVM without a Python boundary, and preserves the validation against the format that the original UDF performed.

The substring built-in is the right replacement because it is the simplest expression that yields the four-character station code, and simpler is better for a code that follows a fixed positional pattern.

The pandas_udf rewrite is the right replacement because vectorised UDFs cross the Python boundary in batches rather than per row, which gives most of the performance gain without changing the regex logic at all.
fields.correctAnswer: The regexp_extract built-in is the right replacement because it expresses the same regex pattern at the Catalyst level, runs in the JVM without a Python boundary, and preserves the validation against the format that the original UDF performed.
fields.rationale:
Of the four candidates, only the regex-based built-in keeps the format check that the original Python implementation gave for free; it runs as a JVM expression with no boundary crossing and matches the same pattern as the UDF. split + getItem (option A) is fast but skips the format validation. substring (option C) is even faster but loses the validation completely. pandas_udf (option D) batches the boundary but does not eliminate it; built-ins are faster still.

When this answer is wrong: If the meter_id format were guaranteed by the upstream contract (no malformed values possible), substring would be the right answer because it gives the largest speedup and the format validation is unnecessary. The exercise's framing (UDF returns null on mismatch implies the engineer expects malformed input) keeps the validation a real requirement.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks split for its structural feel; works but skips the format validation.

Option C: Picks substring for simplicity; fastest of the four but discards the validation the UDF provided.

Option D: Picks pandas_udf for boundary batching; better than per-row UDF but not as fast as a JVM built-in.

fields.label: Why is substring(col('meter_id'), 5, 4) NOT the right replacement here, even though it works on every well-formed meter_id?
options: substring would silently produce a four-character slice for any malformed meter_id (e.g., a meter_id missing the prefix), where the original UDF returns null on a regex mismatch; the substring loses the validation the regex provided.

substring uses 1-indexed positions in Spark's expression engine and the engineer would have to remember the off-by-one convention each time the function appears in the codebase, which is fragile against later edits.

substring on a column of variable-length strings returns null when the string is shorter than the start position, and the meter_id field allows null values that the substring path treats inconsistently with the regex path used by the UDF.

substring requires the engineer to declare the length of the slice as a literal at planning time, which the regex approach handles dynamically through the capturing group's lookup at runtime against the variable input length.
fields.correctAnswer: substring would silently produce a four-character slice for any malformed meter_id (e.g., a meter_id missing the prefix), where the original UDF returns null on a regex mismatch; the substring loses the validation the regex provided.
fields.rationale:
Format validation is what the regex was buying. A non-matching meter_id makes the Python implementation produce null; substring instead returns whatever four characters happen to occupy positions 5–8, regardless of whether the full pattern is satisfied. Replacing the UDF with substring would silently strip the validation step, propagating malformed values downstream. The other options invoke off-by-one risk, length semantics, or planning-time literal requirements that are not the binding issue.

When this answer is wrong: If the upstream system guarantees well-formed meter_ids and the validation is a defensive check that no longer earns its cost, substring becomes the right answer; option B's off-by-one discipline becomes the only remaining concern. The exercise's framing (UDF returns null on mismatch) treats the validation as semantic, not defensive.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names a real but minor concern (1-indexing) as the binding reason; the binding reason is validation loss.

Option C: Reaches for null-handling differences that exist but are not the proximate gap.

Option D: Invents a planning-time literal requirement; substring accepts column expressions for length too.

fields.label: After replacing the UDF with regexp_extract, the engineer measures the new pipeline at 5 minutes total. Which of the original UDF's costs is GONE in the new version?
options: The regex compilation cost, since regexp_extract precompiles the pattern once at planning time and caches it for the duration of the query without re-parsing the pattern on each row of the DataFrame.
The driver-to-executor task dispatch overhead, since the UDF was running on the driver in the original implementation and the built-in expression runs natively on the executor for each partition.

The Python boundary crossing per row, since regexp_extract runs as a Catalyst expression in the JVM and Spark no longer serialises each row to a Python interpreter and back to the JVM during the column derivation.

The garbage collection pressure from the per-row string allocations, since the JVM's string interning pool reuses the four-character station codes across rows in a way the Python interpreter could not match for the original UDF.
fields.correctAnswer: The Python boundary crossing per row, since regexp_extract runs as a Catalyst expression in the JVM and Spark no longer serialises each row to a Python interpreter and back to the JVM during the column derivation.
fields.rationale:
The boundary crossing was the dominant cost (per Q1) and regexp_extract removes it by running in the JVM. The pattern compilation cost (option A) is tiny in either form. The driver-to-executor framing (option B) is wrong: Python UDFs run on executors in Python workers, not on the driver. The GC pressure framing (option D) is real but not the dominant saving.

When this answer is wrong: If the original UDF had run on the driver via collect() and a local map (an anti-pattern), option B's framing would describe a real cost. The exercise's framing (UDF in a withColumn over a DataFrame) places the UDF on executors.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reaches for compilation cost as the saving; both implementations precompile.

Option B: Misplaces the UDF on the driver; UDFs in a DataFrame chain run on executors.

Option D: Names GC pressure as the saving; pressure exists but is not the dominant change.
