tasks.title: When the UDF Is Genuinely Needed

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver enrichment pipeline that calls an external pricing service to compute a tariff-adjusted reading for each row. The UDF wraps an HTTPS request to the pricing service's per-lookup endpoint, which accepts customer_type and region as inputs and returns a price multiplier. The pricing service is owned by another team and is the only authoritative source for the multiplier values. The pipeline runs in 38 minutes, and the lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements proposed by a junior teammate.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is reviewing a Silver enrichment pipeline that calls an external pricing service to compute a tariff-adjusted reading for each row. The UDF wraps an HTTPS request to the pricing service's per-lookup endpoint, which accepts customer_type and region as inputs and returns a price multiplier. The pricing service is owned by another team and is the only authoritative source for the multiplier values. The pipeline runs in 38 minutes, and the lead asks the engineer to evaluate four candidate replacements proposed by a junior teammate.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The pricing service has rate limits (200 requests per second) and the multiplier values change infrequently (a few times per quarter when tariff schedules update). The Silver pipeline runs every 30 minutes against 500,000 rows; calling the service per row exceeds the rate limit and is also wasteful given how rarely values change.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (500,000 rows; columns include customer_type and region; the (customer_type, region) pair has cardinality 16 — 4 customer types × 4 regions)

evidence.label: Udf Implementation
Candidate Replacements
evidence.content:
[
  "Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a small Spark DataFrame at the top of the pipeline and broadcast-join it on (customer_type, region)",
  "Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a Python dict, broadcast the dict to executors, and rewrite the UDF to look up from the dict instead of calling the service",
  "Convert the UDF to mapInPandas so HTTPS calls run in batches per partition rather than per row",
  "Leave the UDF in place but raise the executor count to a level where the rate limit is no longer the binding cost"
]

fields.label: What is the dominant cost of the current implementation, and is it the same kind of cost as POJ5.1's UDF?
options: The dominant cost is the Python boundary crossing per row, the same kind of cost as POJ5.1; replacing with a built-in expression would eliminate it the same way regexp_extract did in the previous exercise.

The dominant cost is the HTTPS call latency per row at 500,000 rows, which is a network-bound cost rather than a CPU-bound or boundary-crossing cost; the previous exercise's pattern does not apply here.

The dominant cost is the network round-trip per row, which is fundamentally external to Spark; the previous exercise's pattern does not apply because the UDF itself is fast and the slowness is in the service call.

The dominant cost is the JSON parsing on each response, which Spark's built-in JSON expressions could replace; the boundary-crossing pattern from the previous exercise applies indirectly through the parse step.
fields.correctAnswer: The dominant cost is the network round-trip per row, which is fundamentally external to Spark; the previous exercise's pattern does not apply because the UDF itself is fast and the slowness is in the service call.
fields.rationale:
The 38 minutes are dominated by waiting on a remote service, not by Python language overhead. POJ5.1's lesson (replace UDF with built-in to remove boundary crossings) does not apply because the UDF is doing genuinely expensive external work, not in-language string manipulation. The right move is to remove the per-row external dependency, not to switch implementation languages. Option B is a partial truth, option A misapplies the previous lesson, and option D names a smaller side cost.

When this answer is wrong: If the pricing service ran inside the same cluster (e.g., a local in-process function call), the dominant cost would shift back to the boundary-crossing pattern and option A would apply. The exercise's framing (HTTPS to an external service) makes the network the dominant cost.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reaches for the previous exercise's lesson without checking whether the cost shape is the same.

Option B: Names the right cost (network) but gives an incomplete framing; the cost is structural, not just a magnitude issue.

Option D: Picks the smaller side cost (JSON parse) and applies the previous lesson loosely.

fields.label: Which of the four candidates is the right replacement?
options: Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a small Spark DataFrame at the top of the pipeline and broadcast-join it on the customer_type and region keys; 16 lookups happen once per run and the per-row HTTPS call disappears.

Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a Python dict and broadcast the dict to executors; the per-row UDF still runs but reads from local memory instead of calling the service, eliminating the network cost while keeping the UDF code structure.

Convert the UDF to mapInPandas so the HTTPS calls run in batches per partition; the per-row latency becomes per-batch latency, and the rate limit is respected because each partition issues one request per its set of unique pairs.

Leave the UDF in place and scale the executor count so the rate limit is no longer the binding cost; the simplest change in code preserves the existing structure and only adjusts the cluster configuration to fit the workload.
fields.correctAnswer: Pre-fetch the 16 multiplier values into a small Spark DataFrame at the top of the pipeline and broadcast-join it on the customer_type and region keys; 16 lookups happen once per run and the per-row HTTPS call disappears.
fields.rationale:
Sixteen unique input combinations and quarter-changing values mean the right structural move is to load all 16 in advance and turn the external dependency into an in-cluster lookup the planner can reason about. The dict approach (option B) works but keeps the UDF and is harder to reason about. mapInPandas (option C) reduces but does not remove the network calls. Scaling executors (option D) just buys the same expensive pattern more capacity; rate limits and the wastefulness of repeated identical calls remain.

When this answer is wrong: If the multiplier values genuinely changed per call (e.g., a real-time pricing service that quotes time-of-day prices), pre-fetching would not preserve correctness and the right answer would shift to option C (batch the calls) or another structural redesign. The exercise's framing (values change a few times per quarter) makes pre-fetch correct.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Picks the dict-broadcast approach for keeping the UDF; introduces unnecessary boundary crossing.

Option C: Picks mapInPandas for batching; reduces network calls but does not eliminate the redundant external dependency.

Option D: Scales the bad pattern; rate limits and waste persist.

fields.label: The teammate proposes the broadcast-dict approach (option B). What is the strongest argument for picking the broadcast-join approach over the broadcast-dict approach?
options: The broadcast-join approach avoids serialising and deserialising the dict on every partition, which adds a one-time cost per task that the broadcast-join pattern handles inside Catalyst's join operator without per-task overhead.

The broadcast-join approach gives Catalyst visibility into the join, which means the join statistics and the dynamic filtering rules apply; the broadcast-dict approach hides the lookup inside a UDF that the optimiser cannot reason about.

The broadcast-join approach keeps the multiplier in a typed Spark column from the start, while the broadcast-dict approach materialises it through a Python UDF that adds the boundary-crossing cost POJ5.1 was about.

The broadcast-join approach scales to larger lookup tables because Catalyst can choose to fall back to a sort-merge join when the table grows beyond the broadcast threshold; the dict approach hard-codes the broadcast model regardless of size.
fields.correctAnswer: The broadcast-join approach scales to larger lookup tables because Catalyst can choose to fall back to a sort-merge join when the table grows beyond the broadcast threshold; the dict approach hard-codes the broadcast model regardless of size.
fields.rationale:
Lookup-table size grows over time. The broadcast-join approach lets Catalyst choose the right join strategy when the table outgrows the broadcast threshold (sort-merge with shuffle, for instance). The dict approach is hard-coded to broadcast and breaks once the dict is too large to ship to every executor. The other options name benefits that exist but are smaller (per-task serialisation cost) or that are actually about correctness/visibility rather than the strongest structural argument.

When this answer is wrong: If the team has a strict guarantee that the lookup will never grow beyond 16 rows, the dict approach's hard-coded broadcast is fine and option B's optimiser-visibility argument becomes the strongest argument. The exercise's framing (no such guarantee) makes scalability the strongest argument.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names a real but smaller cost (dict ser/deser per task); the scalability argument is structurally larger.

Option B: Names a real benefit (optimiser visibility) that is mostly aesthetic at 16 rows; scalability is more concrete.

Option C: Reapplies POJ5.1's lesson when the dict-lookup UDF is much cheaper than the original (no network call).

fields.label: Suppose the multiplier service returns a JSON object with five fields and the engineer needs only one. Should the broadcast-join approach pre-fetch all five fields or only the one?
options: Pre-fetch all five fields and let the join project the one needed; the additional storage is negligible at 16 rows and the team has the option to use the other fields without re-fetching them in a future iteration of the pipeline.

Pre-fetch only the one field needed and let downstream pipelines pre-fetch their own fields if they want different ones; this keeps each pipeline's pre-fetch explicit and avoids a shared-table coupling between teams.

Pre-fetch all five fields but materialise them in a separate reference table that downstream pipelines can broadcast-join against; this turns the pre-fetch into a shared resource without coupling pipelines to one team's choice of fields.

Pre-fetch the one field needed but write a small wrapper that exposes all five so future pipelines can opt in without changing the pre-fetch logic; this lazy approach preserves both the minimum pre-fetch and the future flexibility.
fields.correctAnswer: Pre-fetch only the one field needed and let downstream pipelines pre-fetch their own fields if they want different ones; this keeps each pipeline's pre-fetch explicit and avoids a shared-table coupling between teams.
fields.rationale:
The principle is to pre-fetch what is needed and let other consumers do the same. Pre-fetching all five fields couples this pipeline's lookup decisions to other teams' choices, and the centralised reference-table pattern (option C) is correct only when the team can establish ongoing ownership of a shared resource. Option A's storage argument is true but misses the coupling cost. Option D's wrapper introduces complexity without buying a clear benefit at 16 rows.

When this answer is wrong: If the team owns the multiplier reference table for the platform (a Senior-level concern), pre-fetching all five fields and publishing a shared reference table (option C) becomes the right move. The exercise's framing (Junior level, single-pipeline scope) keeps the per-pipeline pre-fetch the right answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Maximises future flexibility at the cost of present coupling; the storage argument is a footnote.

Option C: Reaches for a platform-level pattern (shared reference table) without the platform-level ownership to maintain it.

Option D: Adds wrapper complexity without a clear benefit; the lazy approach is over-engineered at this scale.

tasks.pssReference: Junior PS9 (Built-in Functions and UDFs), Junior PS7 (Joins and broadcast); Mid PSI3 (broadcast joins); Optimization Cross-Track OPT-J2 lesson 6.
